questions.q: What does the cron schedule `0 2 * * *` mean?
options: Every 2 minutes
Every night at 2:00 AM
Once, 2 hours after the crontab is saved
Every 2 hours, on the hour
questions.explain: The five fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. 0 2 * * * means minute 0, hour 2, every day, every month, every weekday — 2:00 AM nightly.

questions.q: A cron job runs a script with no output redirection at all. What typically happens to its stdout and stderr on most modern servers?
options: It's automatically written to /var/log/cron.log
It's emailed to the user, since mail delivery is enabled by default everywhere
It is effectively lost, since most servers have no mail delivery configured to receive cron's default output
The job fails to run at all without a redirect
questions.explain: Cron's default behavior is to email output, but almost no server has outbound mail configured for this, so unredirected output is effectively discarded -- making failures silent.

questions.q: In `backup.sh >> /var/log/northbridge/backup.log 2>&1`, what would change if `2>&1` were removed?
options: Nothing; it's purely cosmetic
Standard output would still be appended to the log, but error messages (stderr) would not be captured
The script would fail to run
Standard output would stop being logged instead
questions.explain: `>>` alone only redirects stdout. Without `2>&1`, stderr still goes to its default destination (typically discarded under cron), so errors would be missing from the log.

questions.q: What advantage does a systemd timer with `Persistent=true` have over a plain cron entry?
options: It runs the job twice as often automatically
If the system was powered off at the scheduled time, the job still runs once the system is back up, instead of being skipped
It eliminates the need for any logging
It allows the job to run without any service file at all
questions.explain: Persistent=true tells systemd to track whether a scheduled run was missed (e.g. due to downtime) and trigger it on the next boot -- plain cron has no equivalent catch-up mechanism.

questions.q: Why does `nohup some-long-job.sh &` followed by `disown` let the job survive closing the SSH session that started it?
options: nohup and disown both increase the job's process priority
nohup makes the process ignore the SIGHUP signal sent on disconnect, and disown detaches it from the shell's job table
They convert the job into a systemd service automatically
They have no effect on signal handling; only closing the terminal window matters
questions.explain: Closing an SSH session sends SIGHUP to jobs started in it, which normally kills them. nohup makes the process ignore SIGHUP, and disown removes it from the shell's job tracking so it isn't tied to that session.
